strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP question: how persona prompting affects the value-related responses of language models. The proposed protocol is simple, scalable, and interpretable.

The experiments cover seven models from three model families, two questionnaires, and multiple sets of 200 personas. Item-level distributions and aggregate scores support a useful descriptive finding: several response preferences recur under the tested persona generator.

The manuscript provides prompt templates, demographic attributes, questionnaire items, random seeds, exact model identifiers, numerical results, and a code link. These details provide a meaningful foundation for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central inference from convergence to inherent values is unsupported. Resampling personas from the same distribution estimates the same mixture expectation, whose sampling variance decreases with sample size even when personas strongly affect individual responses. Section 4 explicitly rejects this ordinary statistical explanation without justification. Figures 4–5 establish repeatability under a fixed sampling procedure; they do not establish persona-independent, deeply encoded value orientations. This affects the central claim and prevents a positive Findings recommendation in the current version.

The experiments do not sufficiently distinguish model inertia from ineffective steering or properties of the persona distribution. Demographic diversity does not imply uniformly distributed moral judgments. Missing comparisons include repeated responses without personas, repeated responses for fixed personas, and deliberately different persona distributions. Conditional persona-effect analyses, uncertainty estimates, and prompt or answer-order controls would help identify what remains stable. Aggregating responses also does not resolve systematic self-report bias or deception, contrary to the methodological motivation in Section 3.

Questionnaire administration and scoring need clarification. MFQ-30 contains separate relevance and agreement sections, yet Section 3 describes only relevance options, and Table 2 interprets 'Extremely Relevant' as strong agreement. These judgments are not interchangeable. The MRAT description also lacks an explicit centering equation, treatment of the two MFQ dummy items, and the mapping of PVQ-RR items into the ten reported dimensions. These ambiguities affect both score interpretation and reproducibility.

Response parsing is insufficiently validated for the actual experimental setting. Appendix C's human audit covers 89 non-role-play responses from one source model; the selected parser achieves 94.74% accuracy on PVQ-RR. The approximately 800-item comparison does not report a corresponding human-grounded error analysis. A representative audit across models and role-play conditions, with sensitivity analysis, is needed. Missing-data handling also requires explanation: Figure 8 contains totals below 200, and Table 3 omits Claude 3 Opus's third MFQ run.

Several reporting gaps further limit replication and assessment. The abstract promises repeated questions within each persona, whereas Section 3 describes one response per question per persona, leaving the separation of decoding variability and persona effects unclear. API settings are described only as defaults. The contribution beyond cited studies of value stability and persona effects also needs sharper positioning. Targeted controls, corrected interpretation, and clearer experimental reporting could make a next-cycle revision substantially stronger.
